nodes.content: Design an embedded runtime that contains peripheral-driver faults while preserving hard real-time deadlines and safe shared-device recovery.
requirements: Under driver crashes, hangs, and invalid DMA requests, protected control tasks retain 1 ms deadlines.
Recover shared-device service within 50 ms without stale DMA writes or cross-partition state corruption.

nodes.content: Watchdog MPU-isolated drivers below control priority; broker DMA via epoch-scoped IOMMU mappings; fence/reset shared devices before 50-ms restart.
How can outstanding DMA writes be fenced before shared-device restart without blocking protected control tasks?
Asynchronous bus-master quiescence and DMA draining before IOMMU revocation yield zero stale writes, sub-50-ms recovery, and zero deadline misses.
Build asynchronous recovery worker: disable bus mastering, drain or reset DMA, revoke mappings; inject faults and measure deadlines.
Run FaultDMA-10k crash, hang, invalid-DMA, and delayed-write injections under 1-kHz load; log stale writes, deadline misses, and recovery latency.
FaultDMA-10k recorded zero stale writes, zero control deadline misses, zero cross-partition corruptions, and 43-ms worst-case shared-device recovery.
Adopt asynchronous DMA fencing and epoch-scoped mappings: FaultDMA-10k showed zero deadline misses or stale writes, with 43-ms recovery.
Integrate the adopted DMA fencing and epoch-scoped mappings into Runtime v0.3 with a low-priority recovery worker.
Runtime v0.3 firmware includes a low-priority recovery worker, bus-master fencing, DMA drain/reset, and epoch-scoped IOMMU mappings.
On DMA drain timeout, interconnect fencing before IOMMU revocation prevents stale writes without deadline misses or recovery beyond 50 ms.
Extend Runtime v0.3 to fence interconnect before IOMMU revocation; inject 1,000 drain timeouts, measuring stale writes, deadline misses, recovery latency.
Across 1,000 drain timeouts, interconnect fencing yielded zero stale writes or deadline misses, but 71-ms recovery exceeded 50 ms.
Implement per-device interconnect isolation before mapping revocation; bound reset to 35 ms and re-test 1-ms deadlines, stale writes, 50-ms recovery.
Patch Runtime v0.3 with per-device interconnect isolation and 35-ms reset; replay 1,000 drain timeouts, logging stale writes, deadlines, and recovery.
Runtime v0.4 firmware isolates each device before IOMMU revocation, enforces a 35-ms reset timeout, and includes drain-timeout replay logs.
Replay FaultDMA-10k plus 1,000 drain timeouts against Runtime v0.4; measure deadlines, recovery, stale writes, and partition integrity.
Runtime v0.4 replay: zero deadline misses, stale writes, or partition corruptions across 11,000 faults; worst-case recovery 48 ms.
Pin control to core 0 with a 700-µs reservation per millisecond; route driver IRQs and recovery to core 1.
How can driver IRQ storms and recovery work avoid preempting 1-ms control tasks?
Configure Runtime v0.4 with 700-µs core-0 reservation, core-1 IRQs; inject 50-kHz IRQ storms and DMA timeouts; log deadlines, recovery, corruption.
During 50-kHz IRQ storms plus DMA timeouts, recovery reached 62 ms; zero deadline misses, stale writes, or partition corruptions.
Core-1 IRQ saturation causes 62-ms recovery without control deadline misses; throttling driver IRQs to 10 kHz restores sub-50-ms recovery.
Throttle core-1 driver IRQs to 10 kHz, prioritize recovery, then replay 50-kHz storms and measure deadlines and recovery.
Patch Runtime v0.4 with 10-kHz IRQ coalescing and recovery priority; replay 50-kHz storms, measuring recovery, deadline misses, and stale writes.
With 10-kHz IRQ coalescing, storm recovery took 54 ms, still above 50 ms; no deadline misses or stale writes occurred.
Unlike IRQ coalescing alone, reserving 250 µs/ms of core 1 for recovery yields sub-50-ms storm recovery without deadline misses.
Reserve 250 µs/ms of Runtime v0.4 core 1; replay 50-kHz IRQ storms with DMA timeouts, logging recovery and deadlines.
With 250-µs/ms core-1 recovery reservation, storm recovery peaked at 52 ms; zero control deadlines were missed.
Raising core-1 recovery reservation from 250 to 400 µs/ms yields sub-50-ms storm recovery without control deadline misses.
Set Runtime v0.4 core-1 recovery reservation to 400 µs/ms; replay 50-kHz IRQ storms with DMA timeouts, measuring recovery and deadlines.
At 400 µs/ms core-1 reservation, 50-kHz storms with DMA timeouts yielded 47-ms worst-case recovery and zero control deadline misses.
Adopt 400-µs/ms core-1 recovery reservation; 50-kHz storms yielded 47-ms recovery with zero control deadline misses.
Integrate the adopted 400-µs/ms core-1 recovery reservation into Runtime v0.4, retaining core-0 control isolation and IRQ coalescing.
Runtime v0.5 firmware extends v0.4 with a 400-µs/ms core-1 recovery reservation, retaining control isolation and IRQ coalescing.
Does the 700-µs/ms core-0 reservation cover control tasks’ worst-case execution time during driver faults?
Measure control-task execution and core-0 scheduling jitter on Runtime v0.5 during FaultDMA-10k and IRQ storms; compare against 700-µs reservation.
On Runtime v0.5, peak control execution was 612 µs plus 28-µs release jitter, below the 700-µs reservation.
Derive static control WCET and bounded release jitter; compare their sum with the 700-µs reservation and measured 612/28-µs peaks.
Analyze Runtime v0.5 control binaries with aiT 24.04 and the core-0 interrupt schedule; bound WCET-plus-jitter against 700 µs.
Runtime v0.5 timing certificate tightens its core-0 isolation contract: WCET ≤ 655 µs and release jitter ≤ 35 µs.
Audit Runtime v0.5 IRQ affinity and timing certificate; verify 655+35-µs demand fits 700-µs core-0 reservation under storms.
IRQ-affinity audit found driver IRQs confined to core 1; certified 655-µs WCET plus 35-µs jitter fits 700-µs reservation.
Retain the 700-µs/ms core-0 reservation; certified WCET and jitter total 690 µs, and driver IRQs remain on core 1.
Broker shared-device commands through capability-checked per-partition queues; replay only validated, current-epoch shadow state after reset.
Which shared-device state can be replayed after reset without reviving stale DMA descriptors or crossing partition boundaries?
Revalidating partition-owned, DMA-free register shadows after reset while discarding descriptors prevents cross-partition corruption within 50-ms recovery.
Using Runtime v0.5’s timing certificate, fuzz partition-owned shadow replay and stale-descriptor rejection over 5,000 resets; track corruption, deadlines, recovery.
Despite ownership checks, two shared-clock shadow replays corrupted another partition across 5,000 resets; recovery peaked at 46 ms.
Replaying partition-local shadows, recomputing shared clocks from current capabilities, and discarding descriptors yields zero corruptions and sub-50-ms recovery.
Using Runtime v0.5’s timing certificate, fuzz 5,000 capability-checked partition-local shadow replays; recompute clocks, discard descriptors, track corruption, deadlines, recovery.
Across 5,000 resets, capability-checked local replay caused zero corruptions, stale writes, or deadline misses; worst-case recovery was 49 ms.
Adopt capability-checked partition-local replay with shared-clock recomputation; reject shared-clock shadows and DMA descriptors, preserving 49-ms recovery without corruption.
Isolate driver RPC with generation-tagged, bounded queues and fail-fast timeouts; restart faults without blocking control loops.
How can control tasks reject delayed RPC replies from crashed drivers after restart without waiting for device service?
Add per-driver generation tags and eight-entry RPC queues; invalidate generations on restart, discard mismatched replies, and test delayed completions.
Implement eight-entry generation-tagged RPC queues; inject 10,000 delayed post-restart replies, measuring accepted stale replies and control deadline misses.
RPC generation-guard patch provides eight-entry queues, restart-time invalidation, mismatched-reply discard, and 10,000-injection test logs.
Replay 10,000 delayed replies against the generation-guard patch; verify stale-reply rejection, nonblocking RPC, and certified 700-µs control budget.
All 10,000 stale replies were rejected, but restart-held RPC locks delayed control up to 1.12 ms, causing seven deadline misses.
How can restart invalidate RPC generations without holding locks that block 1-ms control tasks?
Atomic generation swaps and lock-free eight-entry RPC queues reject all stale replies while adding ≤10 µs to control latency.
Replace restart-held RPC locks with atomic generation swaps and lock-free eight-entry queues; stress delayed replies and measure control latency.
Patch RPC with atomic swaps and lock-free queues; replay 10,000 delayed replies, measuring stale accepts and certificate-relative latency overhead.
Across 10,000 delayed replies, atomic-swap RPC added 8 µs peak control latency, with zero stale accepts or deadline misses.
Adopt atomic-generation, lock-free RPC: 8-µs peak overhead and zero misses, versus seven misses with restart-held locks.
